content: The relationship between the cumulative duration of breastfeeding and maternal blood glucose levels was analyzed in three studies involving 14,296 participants. The certainty of evidence was rated as very low. Stuebe (2010) examined the impact of breastfeeding duration per child on maternal HbA1C and insulin levels in a study with 89 participants. Thirteen studies (five cohort and eight cross-sectional) investigated the association between breastfeeding duration and maternal hypertension, systolic blood pressure (BP), and diastolic BP. Eleven of these studies were conducted in high-income countries (four in Korea, three in the United States, and one each in Australia, China, Norway, and Poland), while one study each was from upper-middle-income (Brazil) and lower-middle-income (Iran) countries. The age of participants at the time of outcome assessment ranged from 15 to 81 years. There was significant clinical heterogeneity in terms of participant age, ethnicity, studied parameters, outcome definitions, and urban versus mixed residential settings. Five studies (two cohort and three cross-sectional) analyzed the relationship between breastfeeding duration per child and maternal hypertension, involving 262,129 participants. The certainty of evidence was rated as very low. Subgroup analyses for breastfeeding durations of 12–18 months and 18–24 months during the second year of life showed no significant differences in the risk of maternal hypertension. Two studies (one cohort and one cross-sectional) examined the effect of breastfeeding duration per child on maternal systolic and diastolic BP. Lima (2019) also analyzed the impact of cumulative breastfeeding duration on systolic and diastolic BP in a study with 782 participants. A large prospective cohort study by Peters (2017) in China investigated the association between breastfeeding duration per child and stroke risk in parous women aged 35–75 years from urban and rural areas, involving 239,959 participants. Fourteen studies (six cohort and eight cross-sectional) from various countries, including the United States, Korea, Norway, Australia, Brazil, China, Iran, and Poland, reported outcomes related to cardiometabolic health and cardiovascular mortality in women aged 18–85 years in relation to breastfeeding status into the second year. No significant differences were observed when cross-sectional and cohort studies were analyzed separately. The certainty of evidence for these outcomes was rated as very low. Fifteen studies (seven cohort and eight cross-sectional) from countries such as the United States, Korea, Brazil, Finland, Iran, Norway, the Philippines, Poland, and Turkey provided data on maternal anthropometric outcomes in women aged 18–79 years in relation to breastfeeding duration during the second year. No significant associations were found between continued breastfeeding and outcomes such as overweight, obesity, BMI, weight gain, waist circumference, or fat mass. Seven studies (five cross-sectional and two retrospective) examined the association between breastfeeding continuation during the second year and maternal bone health. Four studies were from high-income countries (two from South Korea, one each from Finland and the United States), two from upper-middle-income countries (Turkey), and one from a lower-middle-income country (Iran). The age of participants ranged from 40 to 93 years. No significant differences in bone mineral density (BMD) were observed between women who breastfed beyond the first year and those who did not. Five studies (three cross-sectional and two cohort) analyzed the relationship between breastfeeding duration and BMD of various bones. Minor differences in femoral neck BMD were not statistically significant when subgroup analyses for 12–18 months and 18–24 months were conducted. Dursun (2006) reported no effect of cumulative breastfeeding duration (>12 months vs. 12 months) on lumbar vertebral BMD. A cohort study by Karlson (2004) in the United States examined the relationship between cumulative breastfeeding duration and the risk of rheumatoid arthritis in urban women aged 50–64 years. Li (2020) conducted a cross-sectional study in China to evaluate the association between breastfeeding duration per child (>12 months vs. 12 months) and cognitive function in postmenopausal urban Chinese women aged over 60 years. No studies provided data on the effects of breastfeeding continuation into the second year on maternal fertility or birth spacing. In this systematic review, 146 observational studies were included, with 93 studies providing data on child outcomes and 54 studies on maternal outcomes. Most studies were conducted in high-income or upper-middle-income countries. The certainty of evidence was rated as very low for all outcomes, indicating uncertainty about the benefits or harms of continued breastfeeding into the second year for maternal or child health. The benefits of exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months of life are well-established. However, guidelines recommending continued breastfeeding up to two years or beyond are based on the nutritional value of breast milk and potential maternal benefits, such as reduced cancer risk and prolonged lactational amenorrhea. The evidence for longer breastfeeding durations is less robust and primarily observational, with significant biases and heterogeneity among studies. The findings should be interpreted cautiously, especially for outcomes related to child growth, development, and maternal health. Further research is needed to clarify the potential benefits or harms of continued breastfeeding into the second year.
